cues.text: Class A uses first octets one through one hundred and twenty-six, normally slash eight.
Class B runs from one hundred and twenty-eight to one hundred and ninety-one, slash sixteen.
Class C runs from one hundred and ninety-two to two hundred and twenty-three, slash twenty-four.
Class D, two hundred and twenty-four through two hundred and thirty-nine, is multicast.
Class E, two hundred and forty through two hundred and fifty-five, is reserved or special.
Modern networks use classless addressing, so don't assume the mask from the first octet.

The private address blocks are ten dot zero dot zero dot zero slash eight, one seventy-two dot sixteen dot zero dot zero slash twelve, and one ninety-two dot one sixty-eight dot zero dot zero slash sixteen.
Loopback is one twenty-seven dot zero dot zero dot zero slash eight.
Link-local is one sixty-nine dot two fifty-four dot zero dot zero slash sixteen.
The limited broadcast address is two fifty-five in every octet.
For IPv6, double colon one means loopback; double colon alone is unspecified.
F E eight zero double colon slash ten is link-local, F C zero zero double colon slash seven is unique-local, and F F zero zero double colon slash eight is multicast.
Two thousand double colon slash three is commonly global unicast.
Two thousand and one colon D B eight double colon slash thirty-two is documentation space.
Network address translation, or NAT, translates addresses and often ports.
It is not a substitute for a firewall.
